subject: Agriculture
title: Organic in the Developing World
description: A micro-lesson that makes Organic in the Developing World usable.

hook.text: India has 2.7 million organic farmers—more than any other country. Most farm less than 2 hectares.

buildup.text: In the developing world, many small farmers already farm 'organically by default'—they can't afford chemicals.

discovery.text: Certification lets these farmers access premium export markets—European and US consumers willing to pay more.

twist.text: Certification costs and paperwork burden small farmers. Group certification through cooperatives helps, but adds complexity.

climax.text: Sikkim, an Indian state, became 100% organic in 2016—the first fully organic state in the world.

punchline.text: The world's poorest farmers may lead the organic revolution—if markets reward them.

quiz.question: Which place became the world's first fully organic state in 2016?

details.summary: Organic farming in developing countries presents unique opportunities and challenges. Many smallholder farmers already practice near-organic methods. Certification can open premium export markets but involves costs and infrastructure that disadvantage the poorest producers.
details.whyItMatters: Developing countries account for most of the world's organic farmland by area. Organic certification can transform livelihoods for smallholders, but only if the costs and complexities of certification are addressed equitably.
takeaways: India, Uganda, and Ethiopia lead in number of organic producers worldwide
Many developing world farmers already farm without chemicals due to cost constraints
Participatory guarantee systems offer lower-cost alternatives to formal certification

faq.question: Why is organic farming growing rapidly in developing countries?
faq.answer: Many smallholders already use few or no chemicals because they cannot afford them, making organic certification relatively easy to achieve. Export premiums for organic products significantly increase farmer incomes in countries like India, Ethiopia, and Mexico.

faq.question: What barriers prevent more developing world farmers from going organic?
faq.answer: Certification costs, paperwork requirements, and the need for third-party auditors are significant barriers. Group certification and participatory guarantee systems help, but access to premium markets, training, and organic inputs remain challenges.
